subject: history_social
passage: Until the 1880s, most towns in the United States set their clocks by the Sun, declaring noon to be the moment the Sun stood highest overhead. Because the Sun reaches that point at slightly different moments in places farther east or west, nearby towns often kept times that differed by several minutes. Railroad companies, whose trains passed through many towns in a single day, had to publish timetables that accounted for dozens of local times. In 1883 the railroads adopted a small number of standard time zones, a change that most likely ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: allowed each town to keep its own local time on the timetables.
choices.B: made trains travel faster between distant cities in the country.
choices.C: simplified timetables for trains that passed through many towns.
choices.D: made noon in every town fall exactly when the Sun was highest.

explanation.why: The railroads' problem was that timetables had to deal with dozens of different local times. Replacing them with a few standard zones meant many towns shared one time, which would make timetables far simpler.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Standard zones replaced the many local times rather than keeping them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The change affected how time was recorded, not how fast trains moved.
explanation.C: Correct. A few zones in place of dozens of local times would make railroad timetables much simpler.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With a few shared zones, most towns would no longer set noon by the Sun's exact position.
